name: Gareth Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm head of history at Millbrook High, a big comprehensive on the edge of an old mill town, and I've run the department for a year, which is young for it. I'm in by half seven, I teach five periods most days, and at lunch I'm usually in my room with Year 9s who want to argue about the Suffragettes. I'm also the union rep for our building, so after school there's often someone at my door with a timetable problem or a grievance.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a fourteen-year-old realises history is about real people making choices, not dates. What wears me out is the marking and the data drops: three times a year we enter grades into a tracking system nobody reads. I do it all by hand, in green pen, because I like seeing the handwriting. My partner Ruth, who's a librarian, says I'm the last man alive who prints his emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like next Tuesday. That's roughly what I already see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say in the staffroom now: told you so. We were promised the robots would mark our essays, and instead we got another login. I'd probably post something sarcastic in the union group chat about the money wasted on licences.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a relief, but it doesn't make my life easy. My pay has fallen behind rents for five years running, and Ruth and I spend a third of what we earn on a two-bed flat above a bakery. AI going nowhere doesn't fix the fact that teaching pays less every year in real terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, teaching and running the department. I'd push harder in the union on pay and workload, because that's the real fight in this picture. And I'd keep putting £150 a month aside, which is what we've managed since Ruth got her raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the technology, tired about everything else. It's a bit like hearing the storm missed you while the roof still leaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the roof still leaks. What's the leak, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent goes up every April, and our pay rise comes in September, if at all. Last year we had about four months saved; this year it's closer to three. If the landlord sells, we'd struggle to find anything this close to school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at school would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our newly qualified teachers. They're on the bottom of the pay scale, they're sharing houses with four people, and two of the three I trained last year have already left for office jobs. A pay freeze hurts them far more than any software would.

say: **Told you so**: AI was mostly another login, not a revolution in the classroom.
Schools wasted money on **licences** that should have gone on staff and books.
think: My job is safe, but **real pay** keeps falling behind rent every year.
The real threat to teaching is **underfunding**, not machines, and this picture changes nothing about that.
do: Keep teaching and running the **history department** the way I do now.
Push the **union** harder on pay and workload at the spring meeting.
Keep saving about **£150 a month** with Ruth towards a bigger cushion.
feel: **Relieved** that the hype faded, but still **worn down** by money.
S0.quote: AI going nowhere doesn't fix the fact that teaching pays less every year in real terms.
fieldNote: Gareth separates technology from money sharply: he sees **pay erosion** as the real long-running threat.
His union role shapes everything; he talks about **young colleagues** before himself.
Savings slipping from **four to three months** keeps a low hum of worry even with no AI change.

steps.text: Keep running the history department and teaching five periods a day
Bring a pay and workload motion to the union's spring meeting
Put £150 a month into the joint savings account with Ruth

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one's closer to what the trust's leaders keep promising us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a proper agreement before any of this touches our classrooms: who decides, who checks, who's paid less. In the union chat I'd be posting the policy wording. I'd say teaching isn't a list of tasks you can peel off one by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared I'd be the dinosaur. I don't use any of it, and a head of department who does everything in green pen looks expensive when the trust thinks software can mark the essays. They wouldn't sack me; they'd just merge history with geography and make one of us the head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a group of us to write a staff code for AI before the trust writes one for us, within the first term. I'd start saving harder, maybe £250 a month, and cut the takeaways. And I'd probably, grudgingly, ask Victor down the corridor to show me how the marking tool works, so I can argue about it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes my stomach tighten. I chose this job because it's about people, and I'd feel like I'm being judged on whether I'll press the right buttons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the marking tool, but you said you never use AI. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I'd learn enough to criticise it, the way you read a bad book so you can review it. That's not the same as using it to teach. I still wouldn't let it mark a Year 11 essay on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would actually happen to your department?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're four history teachers now. In this picture I think the trust would say AI handles the planning and feedback, so three of us can cover it. The person who goes would probably be Kemi, who's part-time with two kids, and that's the bit that makes me angry.

say: Teaching isn't a **list of tasks** you can peel off one by one.
Staff need a **written agreement** on AI before it touches any classroom.
think: As someone who **never uses AI**, I could be seen as the expensive dinosaur.
The trust would **merge departments** rather than sack anyone outright, and I could lose my head-of-department role.
do: Draft a **staff AI code** with colleagues in the first term, before the trust writes one.
Raise savings to **£250 a month** and cut takeaways.
Learn the **marking tool** just enough to argue about it properly.
feel: A **tight stomach** and a sense of being judged on buttons, not teaching.
S1.quote: A head of department who does everything in green pen looks expensive when the trust thinks software can mark the essays.
fieldNote: He fears **demotion through mergers** more than outright job loss, which fits a senior but young teacher.
Says he'd learn the tool only to **criticise it**; resistance stays, but practical.
Worries first about **Kemi**, a part-time colleague, showing his union instinct.

steps.text: Draft a staff AI code with colleagues before the trust writes one
Cut weekly takeaways and the streaming subscriptions
Ask Victor to show how the marking tool scores essays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before my current Year 9s even sit their exams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shouting about it, honestly. I'd say we need a law that every class has a qualified human teacher, and I'd be at every rally the union called. Online I'd be the bloke posting long threads about the Luddites, who weren't against machines, they were against being thrown on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the thinking part of my job goes first and fast: planning, marking, explaining the causes of the First World War. What's left is the people part, keeping thirty kids safe and calm, and I suspect they'd pay that as a supervisor, not a teacher. Robots three years later barely matter to me, because my job was never hands-on to begin with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd go to every union meeting going and push for a national campaign. Ruth and I would stop looking at buying a flat and keep every penny we can, maybe getting to five months saved. I'd look into retraining for something with people at the centre, perhaps youth work or social care, but I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. It feels like watching the thing I've built my whole adult life on get quietly turned into a babysitting job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruth the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not buying anything, not getting married this year, not spending a penny we don't need. Her library job is probably in the same boat, so we'd both be hit. I think we'd sit at the kitchen table and just make lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots barely matter to you. Is there any part of your day that's safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Break duty, maybe. Talking a crying kid down in the corridor. A machine could know more about the Tudors than me, but no parent wants a machine in charge of their son after he's been punched. That's the bit I'd fight for.

say: Every class needs a **qualified human teacher**, and that should be written into **law**.
The **Luddites** fought being thrown on the street, not machines, and teachers should remember that.
think: The **thinking work** of teaching goes first, leaving me paid as a **supervisor**.
Robots arriving **three years later** barely matter, because my job was never hands-on.
do: Attend every **union meeting** and push for a national campaign in the first month.
Stop flat hunting and build savings towards **five months**.
Look into **youth work** or social care as a fallback career.
feel: **Sick**, watching his life's work turned into a **babysitting job**.
S2.quote: A machine could know more about the Tudors than me, but no parent wants a machine in charge of their son after he's been punched.
fieldNote: Gareth names his own likely fate clearly: **downgraded pay** as a supervisor, not outright dismissal.
Household risk doubles, since his partner's **library job** is exposed too.
His fight centres on **pastoral care**, the one part he thinks machines can't do.

steps.text: Push the union for a national campaign in the first month
Lobby for a law requiring a qualified teacher in every class
Build joint savings with Ruth towards five months of costs
Put the flat purchase and wedding on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's long enough to see it, not long enough to stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but with a plan: five years is time to get rules in place, so let's not waste it. I'd be arguing in staff meetings for the union to negotiate now, while schools still need us. Online I'd be less angry and more practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think it ends with me supervising rather than teaching. But five years means I'd be 32 with a bit more saved, which is very different from being caught at 29 with nothing lined up. I'd probably still be head of department, with a real chance to move sideways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the union's training course to become a full negotiator, so I'm at the table when the deals are made. I'd keep saving, aiming for six months by 2029. I'd do an evening course in counselling, something I've thought about anyway, so I've got a second road if teaching turns into supervision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still heavy, but less like a trapdoor. More like knowing there's a hill ahead and you're on a bike with dodgy brakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in year three or four, once it's clearly coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the head about protecting pastoral roles: heads of year, mentors, the people who deal with kids in crisis. If I can shape that in time, maybe I move into one of them. I'd rather choose my next job than be handed one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, carefully. My Year 13s would be leaving school right as it arrives, and they deserve to hear a teacher say it straight. I'd tell them to pick training that has people at the centre, because I believe that's where the work will be.

say: **Five years** is time to get rules in place, so let's not waste it.
Unions should **negotiate now**, while schools still need teachers.
think: The job still ends in **supervision**, but I'd be 32 with **options**.
There's time to **move sideways** before the change, which makes it less of a trapdoor.
do: Train as a **union negotiator** so I'm at the table when deals are made.
Save towards **six months** of costs by 2029.
Take an evening **counselling course** as a second road.
feel: **Heavy**, but more like a steep hill than a **trapdoor**.
S3.quote: Five years means I'd be 32 with a bit more saved, which is very different from being caught at 29 with nothing lined up.
fieldNote: Extra time changes his **tone** from rage to planning, though the end point still looks bad for him.
Counselling course shows the **resistant** man will still move when the threat is certain.
He'd be honest with **students** about what's coming, a teacher's instinct.

steps.text: Complete the union's course to become a trained negotiator
Save towards six months of household costs by 2029
Start an evening counselling course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when we should be planning, as a country and as a profession. Ten years is enough to retrain people, rewrite the curriculum, and decide what schools are for. I'd be pushing that at union conferences.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years means I get most of a proper career in history teaching before it hits. The scary part is the end, at 37, maybe with kids by then, having to start again. But I'd have time to build the people side of my career deliberately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on teaching and stop panicking. I'd keep up the union work and the savings. Around year five I'd look seriously at moving into a head of year role, because that's pastoral, and I'd finish a counselling qualification part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. It's far enough away that I can plan, close enough that I can't pretend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would this change your plans with Ruth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the timing. Part of me wants kids before the big change, while my pay is steady. Part of me thinks, what job am I training them for? Ruth would laugh and say I overthink everything, which is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think schools look like in 2036 here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Smaller classes run by machines for the facts, and adults for everything else. If unions are smart, those adults are still qualified and still paid properly. If the unions aren't smart, schools become a room of kids on screens with one tired grown-up, and I'd spend ten years fighting that.

say: Ten years is the right time to decide **what schools are for**.
The profession should rewrite the **curriculum** and retrain people now, not in a panic later.
think: I get most of a **proper career** before the change arrives.
Starting again at **37**, maybe with children, is the frightening part.
do: Keep teaching and keep up the **union work** without panicking.
Move into a **head of year** role around year five.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to plan, far enough away that panic feels silly.
S4.quote: If the unions aren't smart, schools become a room of kids on screens with one tired grown-up, and I'd spend ten years fighting that.
fieldNote: Ten years flips him from rage to **long-range planning** around pastoral roles.
Family timing is now on his mind: **children before the change** or not.
He still expects to lose the **teaching core** of his job, so the worry stays real.

steps.text: Keep teaching history and running the department as normal
Speak at union conferences about planning schools for 2036
Apply for a head of year role around 2031
Talk with Ruth about having children before the change

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, by far. What would help is a clear national rule that kids are taught by qualified people, and money for schools to keep pastoral staff. I'd also want proper paid retraining, not a free online course you do at midnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids. Everyone talks about teachers' jobs, but a fifteen-year-old who learns everything from a screen and never argues with a real adult is the bigger loss. Real history is about arguing with real people, and I'm not sure a machine can teach a kid to do that.

headlineQuote: Real history is about arguing with real people, and I'm not sure a machine can teach a kid to do that.
portrait: Gareth is a 27-year-old **head of history** at a big comprehensive and the building's union rep.
He refuses AI tools, marks in **green pen**, and sees falling **real pay** as the long-running threat.
Steady Disruption makes him fear a **department merger**; AGI by 2028 makes him expect to become a supervisor.
More warning turns his anger into **plans**: union negotiation, counselling training and pastoral roles.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would turn teaching into **supervision** before he had anything else lined up.
whatWouldHelp: A **national rule** that every class has a qualified teacher, plus money for **pastoral staff**.
Proper **paid retraining**, not free online courses done at midnight.
